newsitem.title: ITALY: Netanyahu tells Pope Israel committed on peace.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu tells Pope Israel committed on peace.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Pope John Paul in a letter released on Friday that Israel remained committed to reviving the peace process.
"We are doing all in our power to remove the obstacles to further progress in the quest for peace," Netanyahu said in a letter to the Pope released by Israel's embassy to the Vatican.

Last month the Pope wrote to both Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urging them to revive peace negotiations thrown into crisis by the start of construction in March of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"My government has not allowed negative developments in our region, such as the repeated resorting to street violence, to deter us from continuing the sacred quest for peace," Netanyahu said in his letter, which was undated.
"In effect, our contacts with the Palestinian Authority are continuing, and insofar as it depends on us, will continue.

"It is our earnest hope and prayer that our Palestinian partners will, as the process continues, exhibit the same spirit of responsibility and responsiveness, so that together we shall succeed in achieving the goals to which we are both committed."

Netanyahu thanked the Pontiff for his concern and "your eloquent and candid yet non-intrusive apppeal", which he said was the kind of responsible leadership that was only too rare and a model for appeals by world statesmen to regional leaders.

In his June 16 letter to Netanyahu, the Pope called for "courageous compromises" that would earn him the gratitude of all humanity. In his missive to Arafat, he said the painful history of the past must not prove "vain and useless".
Netanyahu's office said on Thursday that the prime minister was opposing a plan to build dozens of homes for Jews in the heart of an Arab East Jerusalem neighbourhood.

Palestinians have called the plan a "time bomb" that could spark rage similar to the gunbattles which erupted last September when Netanyahu opened an entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem's Old City. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
